retired.text: Notably, several advancements have been made in this field, including the ESM models [ 18 , 10 , 35 , 40 ], ProtTrans [ 3 ], UniRep [ 2 ], ProGen [ 11 , 14 ], and ProtGPT2 [ 4 ], each demonstrating remarkable efficacy in their respective tasks. However, training and deploying these machine learning (ML) models for proteins pose a significant chal- lenge for researchers without ML expertise. These challenges encompass a spectrum of complexities, such as selecting suitable model architectures, managing the nuances of coding, preprocessing extensive datasets, training model parameters, and evaluat- ing or interpreting outputs. Such inherent complexity often serves as a deterrent for non-ML researchers, hindering their active involvement in this domain, particularly in the era when large foundation AI models are increasingly complex.

retired.text: ColabSaprot supports all tasks within the Saprot framework, enabling direct uti- lization for tasks such as zero-shot mutational effect prediction and protein inverse folding. For supervised tasks, users are required to fine-tune ColabSaprot using their own data. We introduce a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique by integrating lightweight adapter networks into the ColabSaprot model (Fig. 2 b) (see Methods). During training, only the adapter parameters in ColabSaprot are updated, resulting in nearly identical accuracy compared to fine-tuning all Saprot parameters (Supple- mentary Fig. 5 ). This design not only enhances optimization efficiency [ 22 , 43 ], but also, more significantly, as first proposed in this work, cultivates collaborative develop- ment of various Saprot models within the research community (Fig. 2 c). Researchers can easily store and exchange their re-trained Saprot models on SaprotHub, accessing existing models by simply loading or uploading adapter networks (Fig. 2 d). Given that adapter networks contain much fewer parameters, often around 1% of Saprot’s, this method significantly reduces storage, communication, and management burdens on SaprotHub, making accessibility and co-construction possible for a broader scientific community.

retired.text: For each mutation dataset, we provide all variants with the wild-type structure, as AF2 cannot distinguish the structural changes induced by single mutations. The Clin- Var dataset only provides UniProt IDs, so we manually downloaded all AF2 structures and eliminated proteins without structures in AlphaFoldDB. Both ProteinGym and Mega-scale datasets provide protein structures, either predicted from AF2 or derived from de novo design.

retired.text: Supplementary Fig. 3 : Case studies of protein inverse folding using Saprot. The blue-colored protein structures are predicted using ESMFold, with residue sequences generated by Saprot, and the green-colored structures are the experimentally deter- mined structures. Given the backbone, Saprot is capable of predicting diverse sequences with few residue overlap while maintaining almost the same 3D structure.
